snippet.title: From Tundra to Table | Two Bulls Down

We appreciate you tagging along for our Alaskan adventure 😀

snippet.title: Paddock Trials: Test Farm Inputs Cheaply
snippet.description:
Farm input trials don’t have to be expensive, complicated, or left to researchers. Here’s how to set up a simple paddock trial so you can test fertiliser, biological inputs and soil products before spreading them across the whole farm.

How do you know if the product you’ve been sold is actually working?

In this Farm Learning video, Tim Thompson is joined by Ben from Greenmate Agriculture to set up a practical paddock trial before applying Humate 9 biological input. The aim is simple: compare a treatment area against a control area, collect a useful baseline, and measure whether the product is actually moving the farm in the right direction.

The video covers how to choose a fair trial paddock, why two similar-looking paddocks are not always equal, how trees, aspect, slope, neighbours and previous management can affect results, and why biological inputs need a longer trial period than many conventional fertiliser responses.

You’ll also see the basic tools used to collect paddock data without spending a fortune: notebook records, photos, soil temperature readings, pH and moisture testing, Brix testing with a refractometer, worm counts, root observations, soil aggregation checks, and repeat sampling across both treatment and control areas.

This is useful for farmers, contractors, landholders, small property owners and anyone using fertilisers, humates, biological inputs, soil amendments, pasture products or regenerative agriculture systems who wants to make better decisions from real paddock evidence.

A good paddock trial helps remove the guesswork. Was it the season? Was it rainfall? Was it soil history? Was it the product? A simple control versus treatment setup gives you a much clearer answer.

This video connects to practical topics including paddock trials, farm input testing, biological farming, soil health monitoring, pasture management, soil pH testing, Brix testing, humate products, regenerative agriculture, soil biology, pasture response, treatment and control plots, and how to measure whether a farm product is working in real-world conditions.

snippet.title: Barbless Barb Wire Explained | Safe Twist Fencing
snippet.description:
What if you could get the performance of barb wire… without the injuries or hassle?
This “barbless barb” might change how you think about fencing.

In this video, we look at Safe Twist wire — a barbless alternative to traditional barb wire — and test how it performs in real-world fencing situations. From ease of tie-off and lower strain on end assemblies, through to visibility and wildlife impact, this is a practical breakdown of whether it actually stacks up on farm.

If you’re building or maintaining fences, running livestock, or trying to reduce wildlife injuries without compromising performance, this is worth a look.

Safe Twist behaves like barb wire where it matters — strain, bounce, and visibility — but removes the sharp barbs that cause injury to stock and native animals. With increasing pressure around animal welfare, biodiversity, and fence longevity, this could be a useful middle ground for many operations.

snippet.title: The Art of Irish Beekeeping: The Keepers | Honey Bee Documentary
snippet.description:
Set against the wild beauty of Ireland’s Beara Peninsula, this intimate documentary follows the De Ruiter family and their deep relationship with the honey bee after 25 years of life and beekeeping in Ireland. From pollen to pot, the film offers a poetic and immersive portrait of the apiary process, revealing how honey is shaped by landscape, season, family knowledge and the fragile rhythms of nature.

Through the family’s daily stewardship, the documentary explores the cultural folklore of bees, the urgent environmental challenges facing pollinators today, and the powerful role conscious human care can play in protecting the natural world. Interwoven with original music and poetry, the film journeys alongside the honey bee and its keepers, uncovering a story of resilience, adaptation, ecology and interdependence.

Both lyrical and grounded, this documentary is a moving celebration of Irish beekeeping, sustainable living, family tradition and the quiet intelligence of the honey bee.

snippet.title: Why Contractors Are Ditching Welded Fence Ends
snippet.description:
Can a bolt-together end assembly replace a welded farm fence end?
Kurt and Amber show the small installation details that make these systems work.

In this Farm Learning episode, Tim visits Gulgong, New South Wales, to look at modern bolt-together fencing end assemblies being used by fencing contractors on their own farm. The discussion covers why post depth matters, why 3 metre end posts are becoming more practical, how to stop collars moving, why stainless threads need copper grease, and how removable end assemblies can help in cropping, stubble grazing, and machinery access.

This video is useful for farmers, fencing contractors, small landholders, graziers, and anyone building stronger farm fencing without relying on welding — especially during fire danger periods or total fire ban conditions.

snippet.title: Who Controls Your Meat? On Farm Abbatoir Update
snippet.description:
Farmers are losing access to abattoirs—and it’s putting entire businesses at risk.
This on-farm solution could change everything.

In this video, we visit a nearly completed on-farm micro abattoir and talk to farmers who are taking control of their processing, profits, and market access.

With over 50 abattoirs lost in the past decade and only limited access to service kills, producers are facing rising costs, long transport times, and increasing risk. But a new model is emerging—small-scale, containerised abattoirs that can be built and run on-farm.

We hear from regenerative farmers, direct-to-market producers, and industry voices about:

Why access to processing is becoming one of the biggest constraints in agriculture
How on-farm abattoirs improve animal welfare, meat quality, and profitability
The real economics—labour savings, value-adding, and business security
What it takes to get approval and build one yourself

This is not theory—this is happening now.

If you’re a livestock producer, regenerative farmer, or small-scale operator looking to build resilience into your business, this is a conversation you need to hear.

snippet.title: Alaskan Style Pemmican, Smoking Caribou Sausage & Winter Ptarmigan Hunt
snippet.description:
A quick trip to the freshly covered snowy mountains in hopes of spotting a winter caribou, no luck with the inclement weather but we did harvest a few ptarmigan for a warm meal back at the cabin. With things settling down a bit, we dig into the freezer and pull out some frozen berries, unrendered fat and caribou meat for sausage. The links go into the smoker for a few hours before packaging and we make a favorite winter treat of ours - pemmican, complete with caribou tallow, waterfowl jerky and Alaskan wild berries.

We appreciate you tagging along for our Alaskan adventure 😀

Thank you for watching and supporting our channel! 💙

snippet.description:

Late winter into the spring riding season didn't quite go our way but that didn't stop us from hitting the unbeaten path. We take a bucket list trip to Denali Highway, visit a glacier and stay at the McLaren River Lodge. We then make our way to a steamy remote hot springs and camp in the Arctic Oven Tent. Long over due for some fishing action we spend the day spearing pike and head into Alaska's backcountry where we end our snowmachine season catching lake trout.
